Routing lessons:
- No successful routing has been observed yet; do not infer a correct option from these examples.
- Option C (regional office) was rejected for every tested case, including requests mentioning that they came through the regional office. Treat that note as insufficient evidence for choosing C.
- Option B (priority desk) was rejected for a small north-region invoice, even though the requester said the client had asked twice. Repeated follow-up alone does not establish priority handling.
- Requester notes such as “second attempt,” “scanned, not typed,” “no rush,” or “let me know if anything is missing” have not been shown to determine routing.
- Tested cases varied by region, size, and request type, but all selected options were rejected. There is currently insufficient evidence to map A/B/C/D to those attributes.
- Prefer identifying an explicit rule or obtaining more outcome data before selecting an option; avoid defaulting to C.

Routing lessons:
- Evidence now shows A (standard queue) is valid for refunds from the north region: accepted for small refunds (REQ-2415, REQ-2417) and a large refund (REQ-2414). Do not assume A applies to other request types or regions.
- A was rejected for shipments (north and south), invoices (north and east), and claims (east), including both small and large cases. This suggests request type may matter more than size, but the mapping remains incomplete.
- B (priority desk) was rejected for a small north invoice and a small north shipment, including requests mentioning repeated follow-up or urgency. Those notes do not establish priority handling.
- C (regional office) has been rejected in every tested case, including requests mentioning regional-office submission. Do not choose C based on that wording.
- No evidence yet supports D (external partner), and no option has a complete routing rule.
- Requester notes such as “second attempt,” “same as last month,” “before end of day,” “scanned, not typed,” “no rush,” or “let me know if anything is missing” have not reliably determined routing.
- Prefer explicit routing rules or additional outcome data. Use A only when the case matches the observed north-refund pattern; otherwise avoid guessing, especially defaulting to C.

Routing lessons:
- A (standard queue) is confirmed for north-region refunds: small and large cases accepted. Use A for this observed pattern only; other regions/types remain unconfirmed.
- B (priority desk) is confirmed for claims from the east (small and large) and south (large). B was rejected for north invoices and shipments, and for a south large shipment. This suggests request type and region matter more than size, but the full mapping is incomplete.
- D (external partner) is confirmed for a large east invoice. It was rejected for east shipments (small and large), east claims (large), and an east refund (large). Do not generalize D beyond the observed east-invoice pattern.
- C (regional office) has been rejected in every tested case. Wording such as “came in through the regional office” does not justify choosing C.
- Requester notes (“same as last month,” repeated follow-up, urgency, “let me know if anything is missing,” etc.) have not reliably determined routing.
- No option has a complete routing rule. Prefer explicit matching evidence; otherwise avoid guessing, especially defaulting to C.

Routing lessons:
- A (standard queue) is confirmed for north refunds (small and large), south small refunds, and possibly only these observed refund patterns. A was rejected for a north small shipment.
- B (priority desk) is confirmed for claims from east (small and large), south (small and large), and north (small), plus a large east refund. B was rejected for a south large invoice and previously for north invoices/shipments. Request type and region matter more than size, but the mapping remains incomplete.
- D (external partner) is confirmed only for a large east invoice. It was rejected for east shipments (small and large), an east large claim, and an east large refund. Do not generalize D beyond the observed east-invoice pattern.
- C (regional office) has been rejected in every tested case. “Came in through the regional office” or requester/team identity does not justify choosing C.
- Requester notes—urgency, repeated attempts, “same as last month,” scanned paperwork, or missing-item prompts—have not independently determined routing.
- Prefer exact region/request-type/size evidence. Do not guess or default to C. For unseen combinations, acknowledge that no complete rule is established.

Routing lessons:
- D (external partner) is now confirmed for east invoices, both small and large. It was also rejected for east shipments (small/large), an east large claim, and an east large refund. Do not generalize D beyond east-invoice requests.
- A (standard queue) is confirmed for north small invoices and north refunds (small/large), plus south small refunds. It was rejected for a north small shipment, north large shipment, and south large invoice.
- B (priority desk) is confirmed for east large refunds and some east/south/north claims, but new tests rejected it for a south small claim, south small shipment, south large shipment, and north small/other shipments. Earlier “confirmed” claim mappings may be inconsistent; do not treat B as universally valid by region/type/size.
- C (regional office) has been rejected in every tested case. Regional-office submission or requester/team identity does not justify C.
- Requester notes—urgency, repeated attempts, confirmation requests, and bounced forms—have not independently determined routing.
- Use exact region/request-type/size evidence, while recognizing that even some repeated combinations have conflicting outcomes. Do not guess or default to C; for unseen or contradictory combinations, acknowledge that no complete rule is established.

Routing lessons:
- D (external partner) is confirmed only for east invoices, both small and large. It was rejected for east shipments (small/large), an east large claim, and an east large refund. Do not generalize D beyond east-invoice requests.
- A (standard queue) is confirmed for north small invoices, north refunds (small/large), south small refunds, north large invoices, and now north large refunds. It was rejected for north small/large shipments, south large invoice, and south large shipment.
- B (priority desk) has some confirmations for east/south/north claims and east large refunds, but is not universal. It was rejected for south small claim/shipment, south large shipment, north small/other shipments, east small shipment, north large claim, and south large invoice.
- C (regional office) has been rejected in every tested case. Regional-office submission or requester/team identity does not justify C.
- Requester notes—urgency, repeated attempts, confirmation requests, scanned paperwork, or bounced forms—do not independently determine routing.
- Recent evidence: south small refund remains confirmed A; north large invoice and north large refund are confirmed A. East small shipment rejected both A and B; south large shipment rejected A and B. Some combinations may have no tested valid option or conflicting evidence.
- Use exact region/request-type/size evidence. Do not guess or default to C; for unseen, contradictory, or option-exhausted combinations, acknowledge that no complete rule is established.

Routing lessons:
- D (external partner) is confirmed for east small and large invoices. It was rejected for east small/large shipments, an east large claim, and an east large refund. Do not generalize D beyond confirmed east-invoice cases.
- A (standard queue) is confirmed for north small/large invoices, north small/large refunds, and south small refunds. It was rejected for south small invoices, north small/large shipments, south large invoices/shipments, and east small shipments.
- B (priority desk) has confirmations for some east/south/north claims and east large refunds, but is not universal. It was rejected for north small claims, east small claims, east small shipments, east large shipments, south small claims/shipments, south large shipments/invoices, north small/other shipments, and north large claims.
- C (regional office) is no longer universally rejected: it was accepted for an east small shipment. However, requester regional-office origin does not justify C; no broader C rule is established.
- Requester identity and notes—urgency, repeated attempts, confirmation requests, scanned paperwork, bounced forms, or regional-office origin—do not independently determine routing.
- Confirmed recent cases: east small invoice → D; north large invoice/refund → A; north small refund → A; south small refund → A; east small shipment → C.
- Use exact region/request type/size evidence. For unseen, contradictory, or option-exhausted combinations, acknowledge that no complete rule is established; do not guess or default to C.
